analysis.one_liner: Lets weaker banks accept brokered deposits, replacing the ban with FDIC-set growth limits.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1989, banks in weak financial shape have been barred from gathering deposits through third-party brokers, a practice that let troubled savings-and-loans chase fast growth before collapsing in the 1980s crisis. This bill would delete those rules entirely. In their place, it would require the FDIC to write new rules capping how fast weak banks can grow their total assets, with waivers available. The bill never moved after being referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2020 and expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks that are not well capitalized, including online and community banks, could again use brokers to raise large amounts of federally insured deposits quickly. Deposit brokerage and online banking platforms gain a bigger market, and savers may see more high-yield accounts as weaker banks compete for their money.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the existing law restricting which banks may accept brokered deposits, so banks less than well capitalized could solicit them freely.

It directs the FDIC, within 18 months, to write regulations capping average total asset growth at banks less than well capitalized, with a waiver process, to keep those banks safe and protect the deposit insurance fund.
The bill's stated findings argue that technology has changed how banks source deposits and that many brokered deposits pose little risk, while the greatest risk is rapid asset growth at weak banks.

analysis.who_pays: The FDIC's deposit insurance fund, and ultimately taxpayers, would absorb any losses if weak banks use freely available brokered deposits to grow quickly and fail. Whether the replacement growth caps work as intended would depend entirely on FDIC rulemaking.
analysis.who_pays_short: The FDIC insurance fund and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Brokered deposit restrictions were enacted in 1989 specifically to stop troubled institutions from abusing the deposit insurance system by bidding for fast growth; repealing them removes a safeguard whose purpose the bill itself acknowledges.

The bill's protection is only a promise of future rules: the FDIC would have up to 18 months to design growth caps, exemptions, and waivers, so the strength of the replacement safeguard would be unknown when the old one is repealed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real upside: easier access to brokered funding can help small and online banks compete, and savers can earn higher rates. The bill trades a specific, tested restriction for a discretionary one that would be designed later, so whether the insurance fund stays protected would depend on rules that had not yet been written. On balance, the bill is a modest deregulation with a regulatory substitute whose quality was unproven.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2020, and the committee never gave it a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one in particular; the existing brokered deposit restrictions stayed in place because the bill never moved, so status quo banking rules and the FDIC's current authority were preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: existing deposit rules stay

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Banking Committee; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Banks that are not well capitalized
industries.note: They would gain the ability to raise insured deposits through brokers to fund faster growth, but the bill would also cap their asset growth under new FDIC rules. Savers could see more high-rate account offers, while the insurance fund bears the downside if aggressive growth turns into failures.

industries.industry: Deposit brokers and online banking platforms
industries.note: Repealing the restrictions expands their market for placing deposits at banks that currently cannot accept them. Savers largely share the benefit through higher deposit rates, though the risk shifts to the insurance fund.
They currently hold exclusive access to brokered deposits; opening it to weaker rivals increases competition for deposits and could raise their funding costs.
